intro: Walk into almost any skatepark and you will hear it: the long, rough scrape of metal trucks on a steel-capped ledge, or the hiss of a deck sliding across a waxed rail. Grinds and slides began on the rounded coping of empty pools in the late 1970s. After skaters learned to ollie on flat ground in the early 1980s, they carried those tricks to curbs, ledges and rails everywhere.

This unit has two halves. The first teaches the tricks step by step, starting on a low painted curb or flat bar with a helmet, wrist guards and knee pads: the 50-50, the 5-0, the boardslide, the noseslide and the tailslide, plus how to approach, where to look and how to bail. The second half explains the physics underneath every grind: the friction force, the normal force, how fast a grind slows and how far it goes.

By the end, you will be able to explain each trick's steps with front foot and back foot, and use f = μN, a = μg and d = v²/(2μg) to predict how far a board will slide. You will also see why a little wax or a little more speed can make a grind go so much farther.
bigQuestion: How do skaters use balance, speed and friction to ride along an edge, and how can physics predict how far they will go?

timeline.t: Isaac Newton publishes the Principia, with his laws of motion
Guillaume Amontons reports that sliding friction grows with the load
Andrew Motte's English translation of the Principia is published
Larry Stevenson is granted a patent for the kicktail
Frank Nasworthy's urethane Cadillac Wheels give boards grip and speed
Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City open as the drought empties pools
Skaters grind the coping of empty backyard pools; Alan Gelfand's ollie appears
Rodney Mullen brings the ollie to flat ground, opening curbs and ledges
Skaters begin building Burnside skatepark under a bridge in Portland, Oregon

words.d: a trick in which one or both metal trucks scrape along an edge or rail
a trick in which the wooden underside of the deck rubs along an edge or rail
a grind with both trucks on the edge at once
a grind on the back truck only, with the nose up
a slide with the board crosswise on a rail, the middle of the deck sliding between the trucks
a slippery coating rubbed on an edge to lower friction
to leave the board on purpose when a trick goes wrong
a force between touching surfaces that pushes against their sliding
a surface's push on an object, at a right angle to the surface
the number μ that tells how strongly two surfaces resist sliding
acceleration that slows an object down; on a level rail it equals μg
the energy of motion, KE = ½mv², which friction turns into heat

test.q: Which part of the board touches the edge in a 50-50?
test.why: A 50-50 grinds on both trucks at once.

test.q: Which obstacle is right for a first grind?
choices: a low painted curb at a skatepark
test.why: Start low and away from cars.

test.q: In a 5-0, the board stops because the tail drags. What is the fix?
test.why: Tail drag comes from too much weight back, so move it a little forward.

test.q: Which trick sets only the tail on the ledge with the board turned a quarter turn?
test.why: A tailslide rests the underside of the tail on the ledge.

test.q: Where should your eyes be during a grind?
choices: on the end of the ledge
test.why: Your body follows your eyes, so look at where you will exit.

test.q: What is the safest bail when a grind stops short?
choices: step off with both feet and jog it out
lock your arms and catch yourself
test.why: Stepping off puts you on your feet without falling.

test.q: Why should you approach a ledge at a shallow angle?
choices: so the board goes over the ledge
so you go slower than walking
so the trucks can lock on instead of hitting the edge
test.why: Riding straight at it slams the board into the edge or over the top.

test.q: What does μ stand for in f = μN?
test.why: μ is the coefficient of friction, a number with no unit.

test.q: A 60 kg skater grinds with μ = 0.30. What is the friction force?
On a level rail, what is the slowing of a grind with μ = 0.30?
Why does a heavy skater slow at the same rate as a light skater on the same ledge?
choices: more weight gives more friction but also more mass to slow
test.why: In a = μmg divided by m, mass cancels.

test.q: A board starts at 2.0 m/s with μ = 0.30 (2μg = 5.88). How far does it grind?
Two skaters arrive at the same speed. One edge has half the μ of the other. How do their grinds compare?
choices: the slicker edge gives twice the distance
the slicker edge gives half the distance
the slicker edge gives four times the distance
test.why: μ is on the bottom of d = v²/(2μg), so halving μ doubles d.

test.q: What happens to the board's kinetic energy as friction stops a grind?
test.why: Friction turns motion energy into heat and a little sound.

test.q: Why does a steel ledge cap usually give a longer grind than bare concrete?
choices: steel is smoother, so its coefficient of friction is lower
test.why: Concrete's sand and stones catch the trucks; smooth steel lets them slide.

write.prompt: Explain how to do a 50-50 on a low curb, step by step, using front foot and back foot. Then use a worked example with d = v²/(2μg) to show how far the grind would go at a speed you choose, and explain what would change with wax or more speed.
tips: Start with safety and the right spot: gear on, a low curb, no cars.
Write each step in order with First, Next and Then.
Show every step of the arithmetic, with units.
Label your coefficient of friction as an example value.
End by comparing two cases, such as waxed and bare, or slow and fast.
